title: Dense Layers – The Workhorse 🐴
description: Deep dive into fully connected layers: weights, biases, and output computation.

slides.title: Dense = Fully Connected 🔗
slides.content:
# Every Neuron Connects to Every Neuron in Previous Layer

A **Dense layer** (also called Linear or Fully Connected) performs:
```
output = activation(dot(input, weight) + bias)
```
- `weight`: matrix of shape `(input_dim, units)`
- `bias`: vector of shape `(units,)`

> Analogy: A round‑table discussion where every person shares their opinion with everyone at the next table.

slides.title: Creating a Dense Layer
slides.codeSnippet:
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense

# 32 neurons, ReLU activation
layer = Dense(32, activation='relu')

quizData.question: If input has 100 features and a Dense layer has 64 units, what is the shape of its weight matrix?
quizData.explanation: Weights multiply `input (batch,100)` by `(100,64)` to get `(batch,64)`. So weight shape = (input_dim, units).

slides.title: Weights & Biases Initialization 🎲
slides.content:
# Starting Values Matter

By default, Keras uses:
- **Weights**: Glorot uniform (also called Xavier).
- **Biases**: zeros.

You can change it:
```python
Dense(64, kernel_initializer='he_normal', bias_initializer='zeros')
```

Proper initialisation helps training converge faster.

slides.title: Inspecting Weights
slides.content: After building the model, you can see weight shapes:
slides.codeSnippet:
model = Sequential([Dense(32, activation='relu', input_shape=(100,))])
model.build((None, 100))  # explicit build
weights, biases = model.layers[0].get_weights()
print('Weight shape:', weights.shape)  # (100, 32)
print('Bias shape:', biases.shape)     # (32,)

slides.title: Parameter Count 📊
slides.content: Number of parameters in a Dense layer = `input_dim * units + units` (weights + biases). For 100 inputs and 64 units: 100*64 + 64 = 6464.
